transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Redwood: Jordan Lee, Priya Nair | BrightHealth AI: Carlos Mendes, Aisha Khan, Tom Brewer

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on runtime performance tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted and Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments. Discussed latency/throughput, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization impacts, noisy neighbor isolation, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps: benchmarks, pricing, compliance docs, pilot planning.

Topics: runtime perf, latency vs cost, throughput guarantees, KV cache TTL, batching windows, quantization accuracy/cost tradeoffs, VPC and on-prem feasibility, data residency, SOC2/KMS, canary rollouts

[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive on dedicated vs hosted — i'm joined by priya our se who will drive the perf sections. how's the morning folks?
[00:12] Carlos Mendes: good thanks, excited to dig in. got a handful of questions specifically around noisy neighbor and throughput guarantees.
[00:18] Aisha Khan: yeah, and we have a particular workload: conversational triage, ~600 rps peak during business hours, avg 256 token context, 512 tokens in responses for LLM reply — we want p95 latency under 200ms if possible.
[00:30] Priya Nair: okay, good to know. quick clarification — when you say 600 rps is that concurrent requests or total qps?
[00:35] Aisha Khan: that's requests per second, roughly 40 concurrent sessions but arrival is spiky, lots of bursts.
[00:43] Tom Brewer: also our security posture requires VPC connectivity and KMS integration for keys if we go private.
[00:50] Jordan Lee: noted. we'll walk through runtime assumptions. priya, take it away.

[01:00] Priya Nair: great thanks. firstly, high level: hosted mode — multi-tenant sealed environment, great for bursty traffic and quick start, pricing optimized for pay-as-you-go. Dedicated — reserved GPU pools, you get tenant isolation and capacity guarantees. Private/VPC means you run a customer-controlled control plane and optionally on-prem for compliance.

[02:05] Priya Nair: for latency/throughput there's a couple of levers: batching, KV cache (prefix caching / KV cache warm), and model quantization. Batching increases throughput and reduces cost, but it increases per-request latency depending on batching window. KV cache can avoid recomputing prefix keys and saves a lot for conversational workloads with repeated contexts.

[03:10] Carlos Mendes: about KV cache — do you store per-conversation KV caches in hosted? what's the eviction policy? are they shared?
[03:22] Priya Nair: in hosted we do per-customer logical KV entries, but physical memory is shared; eviction is LRU with TTLs configurable per deployment tier. for dedicated, you control the pool so you can provision more KV memory and tweak TTLs; on-prem obviously you control the full lifecycle. note: exact semantics vary by model architecture — some older models have bigger KV footprints per token.

[04:05] Aisha Khan: LRU with TTL — okay, but noisy neighbor concerns come up if others fill up the KV memory in hosted right?
[04:12] Priya Nair: yes, in hosted noisy neighbor can manifest as increased eviction rates if a shared node's memory gets saturated. we mitigate with soft quotas, but it's not the same as dedicated physical isolation. that's one of the key rationale for dedicated/dedicated+private.

[05:00] Tom Brewer: throughput guarantees — can you promise consistent p95 under load in dedicated? we're trying to size for worst-case business hours.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: dedicated gives SLA-backed throughput targets if you commit to reserved capacity. we define throughput in tokens/sec per GPU profile and provide autoscaling/burst capacity options. importantly, SLA covers availability and configured latency SLOs within the reserved pool.

[06:02] Priya Nair: to add, we measure throughput by synthetic benchmarks and per-model profiling: GPU type, sequence length, kv-cache hit ratios all factor in. the dedicated pool prevents other customers from contending for GPU and KV memory, so p95 variability is much lower.

[07:00] Carlos Mendes: what's the delta in cost roughly between hosted burstable and reserved dedicated for our footprint? ballpark is fine.
[07:08] Jordan Lee: ballpark for your 600 rps with mixed token lengths — hosted might be higher per-token due to multi-tenant overhead but no reserved cost; dedicated has fixed monthly commit plus lower per-token infer cost. we'll share the pricing sheet — but rough ballpark dedicated can be 30-50% cheaper at scale depending on model/quantization.

[07:50] Aisha Khan: quantization — we rely on FP16 today but are open to int8/4-bit if accuracy is acceptable. how does Redwood handle quantization and accuracy regressions?
[08:05] Priya Nair: we support several quantization profiles; we run end-to-end evals against your prompt set as part of the onboarding pilot. typical impact: int8 often reduces memory and improves throughput with small accuracy delta; int4 is aggressive but may need validation. Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per workload.

[09:02] Tom Brewer: any difference in available quantized kernels between hosted and dedicated? sometimes cloud providers limit low-bit kernels.
[09:12] Priya Nair: for hosted we can deploy optimized kernels on our fleet, but in dedicated you have more control on kernel versions and can enable the most aggressive kernels if the hardware supports it. on-prem is fully controlled by you so you can build with custom backend libs too.

[10:00] Speaker 1: (overlap) we also —
[10:05] Jordan Lee: sorry, that was a bit of crosstalk. 

[10:12] Priya Nair: another key piece is batching strategy: fixed-time windows vs adaptive batching. fixed windows cap latency but can underutilize GPUs if traffic sparse. adaptive batching groups by sequence length and dynamic thresholds to maximize utilization without blowing up tail latency. Dedicated pools allow us to tune batch sizes aggressively as you control the capacity profile.

[11:05] Aisha Khan: do you expose batch size controls per route or is that internal?
[11:12] Priya Nair: we expose batching configs in the route config for dedicated and private — you can set max batch size, max wait ms, and we provide recommended starting points. hosted has sensible defaults and some tiered knobs but not full route-level control for safety in multi-tenant.

[12:00] Carlos Mendes: about the KV cache warm-up — how do you warm caches after failover or deploys? if we have a canary rollout with model change we need to avoid cold-starts at high traffic.
[12:12] Priya Nair: good question. for rollouts we support staged warming: pre-warm with synthetic requests, live traffic mirroring to the canary, and background prefetching for commonly used prefixes. for dedicated you can retain warmers across nodes more reliably. hosted relies on warm-up heuristics and cross-node cache sharing where applicable.

[13:00] Aisha Khan: what's the expected latency hit on cold KV? if a prefix is cold do you recompute entire KV from scratch each time?
[13:10] Priya Nair: cold KV means you compute base layers again, so per-token cost increases. in practice we've seen 2-5x token compute delta on cold start for long contexts, so warming is important for strict p95 constraints.

[14:00] Tom Brewer: security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs — hosted meets SOC2, but for KMS with hosted can we bring our own key?
[14:12] Jordan Lee: hosted uses Redwood-managed KMS by default, but for enterprise customers we support BYOK via customer-managed KMS in dedicated/private, and in some dedicated-hosted hybrid models. we'll share the SOC2 docs and KMS integration guide.

[15:00] Carlos Mendes: data residency — some PHI-related data may require EU residency. how do you handle region pinning?
[15:08] Jordan Lee: we can pin dedicated/private pools to regions; hosted supports region selection but not guaranteed tenancy unless you go dedicated in that region. private/on-prem obviously gives full control over residency.

[16:00] Priya Nair: addressing noisy neighbor more technically: in hosted we rely on cgroups, soft reservations, and scheduler heuristics to isolate CPU/GPU/esp. memory. but memory pressure and KV eviction are visible at the tenant level. dedicated maps your workloads to dedicated instances so interference is negligible.

[17:12] Aisha Khan: do you have observed p95 variance numbers? any bench numbers to cite?
[17:22] Priya Nair: yes — rough internal numbers: hosted p95 variance can be up to 40-60ms under certain burst patterns for small models; dedicated reduces that variance to ~10-15ms for same config due to isolation and reserved KV. that assumes similar hardware and quantization. we'll include more concrete numbers from today's follow-up benchmark.

[18:30] Carlos Mendes: can we run a quick hypothetical: if we move to int8 quantized model on dedicated with batch window 10ms and KV hit rate 85%, what does throughput look like?
[18:45] Priya Nair: rough back-of-envelope: with int8 you often get ~1.8-2.5x throughput improvement vs FP16 depending on kernel. with batch window 10ms and 85% KV hits, tokens/sec can increase proportionally. we'll model this in the benchmark spreadsheet for your exact model & sequence lengths.

[20:00] Tom Brewer: what's the recovery behavior on GPU preemption or node failure in dedicated? do you failover to other nodes in the pool or spill to hosted?
[20:12] Jordan Lee: dedicated pools have intra-pool replication and we support automated fallback policies — you can fail over to a standby node in the same pool; alternatively we can configure cross-pool fallback to hosted as a safety net but that depends on your compliance posture. failover will incur cold KV and warm-up cost.

[21:30] Aisha Khan: how long to spin up a dedicated pool if we commit? we want to plan procurement timelines.
[21:38] Jordan Lee: typical lead time is 2-4 weeks for a standard dedicated pool depending on GPU types and region; on-prem is longer due to procurement and install. for urgent needs we offer burst capacity on hosted while dedicated provisioning completes.

[22:40] Priya Nair: i wanted to surface one subtlety: long-token contexts can exacerbate KV memory growth. for some models the per-token KV size is higher and quantization doesn't change KV footprint. so capacity planning must account for context-length distribution.

[23:58] Carlos Mendes: noted. our contexts are 256 average but we have occasional 2k token back-and-forths for diagnostics — how should we handle that?
[24:09] Priya Nair: two approaches: 1) tier long-context requests to a different route with dedicated nodes sized for longer KV; 2) offload long history to retrieval-augmented chunks so runtime per-request KV remains small. both are viable; we can show examples.

[25:30] Aisha Khan: on the topic of observability, what metrics do you expose for per-route latency and KV hit rates?
[25:38] Jordan Lee: Redwood Console exposes per-route token counts, p50/p95/p99 latencies, KV hit/miss ratios, batch sizes, GPU utilization and per-token cost estimates. logs include request traces and audit logs if enabled.

[26:40] Tom Brewer: regarding on-prem deployment, how opinionated is the stack? we run k8s with strict security baselines.
[26:50] Priya Nair: on-prem is a packaged deploy but supports k8s (we support helm charts / operators). we integrate with customer KMS and SSO; team work with your infra during onboarding to validate security configurations. air-gapped options require a slightly longer setup but are supported.

[28:00] Jordan Lee: i want to call out cost-control levers: you can set per-route quotas, model fallbacks to smaller variants, and cache TTLs that reduce compute. Redwood Optimize gives automated suggestions for batching and quantization to hit cost targets while maintaining eval scores.

[29:12] Carlos Mendes: about fallbacks — is function/tool calling supported across variants? i.e., can we call a cheaper model for standard replies and fall back to a higher-cost model for risky cases?
[29:22] Priya Nair: yes, we support routing policies and automatic fallbacks. you can define confidence thresholds to escalate to a higher-fidelity model. routing can be region-aware too.

[30:00] Speaker 2: (minor audio)

[30:15] Priya Nair: for the benchmark plan i propose: 1) Priya will get a representative prompt set and traffic profile from you, 2) run hosted and dedicated (reserved) runs with FP16, int8, and experimental int4, 3) capture p50/p95/p99, KV hit ratios, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens, 4) produce a recommendation.

[31:00] Aisha Khan: that sounds good. timeline?

[31:05] Priya Nair: aim to run within 5 business days after we get the sample data; so target by 2025-10-20.

[31:30] Carlos Mendes: one more question on legal/procurement — for dedicated do you require an enterprise contract or can we do a monthly commitment initially?

[31:42] Jordan Lee: we have flexible commit options; monthly or annual reserved capacity. for larger enterprises we do standard enterprise agreement negotiations, but smaller pilots can start with shorter commits. we'll have pricing in the sheet.

[32:20] Tom Brewer: what about upgrades/patches on dedicated? do you manage runtime upgrades or is that customer-controlled?

[32:28] Priya Nair: for Redwood-managed dedicated we handle runtime upgrades within maintenance windows you approve; for private/on-prem you control patching or we can partner to operate under an ops contract.

[33:40] Aisha Khan: couple of smaller things — logging retention and audit logs, are they configurable per pool?

[33:48] Jordan Lee: yes, retention is configurable; audit logs can be exported to your object store or SIEM. retention durations depend on plan due to storage cost.

[34:30] Carlos Mendes: competitors — we looked at AWS SageMaker endpoints and a self-hosted runtime. main gap was orchestration and per-token cost. did you see similar?

[34:40] Jordan Lee: customers often choose Redwood when they want the balance of performance + ops features without building orchestration. we'll send side-by-side notes comparing to the vendors you mentioned.

[35:10] Priya Nair: small note on model memory and quantization: for some models int8 kernels are memory-bound improvements; for others int4 changes compute patterns and you must validate eval metrics. Redwood provides eval harnesses to run your scoring sets.

[36:05] Tom Brewer: about network egress — in hosted if we route logs to our s3 in eu-west-1, do you charge egress?

[36:16] Jordan Lee: egress charges depend on region and outputs; typically customers are billed for egress out of Redwood-managed regions. for private deployments egress is internal to your network. we'll add estimated egress numbers in the pricing pack.

[37:20] Aisha Khan: are there customer references for similar workloads in healthcare? PHI considerations are sensitive.

[37:28] Jordan Lee: yes we have a couple of enterprise customers in regulated spaces on dedicated and private options — we'll connect you to a reference under NDA.

[38:00] Priya Nair: technical caveat — if you plan to do long-running KV sessions for diagnostic traces, ensure your KV memory headroom is sized; otherwise cold starts will spike latency. we can model this in the benchmark.

[39:15] Carlos Mendes: would you be able to run an A/B test of routing policies during the pilot? e.g., 80% traffic to dedicated node pool, 20% to hosted?

[39:26] Priya Nair: yes, we support traffic splitting and can do canary-style rollouts. that will help quantify delta in latency/cost for your exact traffic.

[40:10] Tom Brewer: any additional operational costs for dedicated e.g., runbook support?

[40:18] Jordan Lee: there are optional support tiers; standard includes monitoring and alerts, premium includes dedicated SE time and on-call support. we'll outline support tiers in the follow-up.

[41:05] Aisha Khan: quick question — what's the recommendation if we need lowest possible latency under 100ms p95?

[41:12] Priya Nair: to hit p95 <100ms you likely need local co-located inference (private/on-prem) with high-end GPUs, aggressive quantization, and very high KV hit rate plus small batching windows. dedicated in-region with reserved GPUs may reach near 100ms for smaller models, but for stricter SLOs on larger contexts on-prem gives best control.

[42:10] Carlos Mendes: got it.

[42:30] Jordan Lee: recap — action items: pricing + SOC2/KMS docs from jordan, priya to run benchmark plan, schedule on-prem sync with tom and samir; propose pilot dates. any other open items?

[43:00] Mei Li: can you include the console screenshots and specific dashboard metrics in the follow-up? that helps our compliance team.

[43:08] Jordan Lee: yes, we'll include console screenshots, metric definitions, and retention policies.

[44:00] Aisha Khan: thanks, that's helpful. one note: please include the exact kernel versions you plan to run in the benchmark results.

[44:12] Priya Nair: will do, we'll record kernel versions and GPU SKUs.

[45:00] Carlos Mendes: thanks everyone, appreciate the detail.

[45:05] Jordan Lee: thank you — we'll follow up with the slides, pricing and benchmark plan.

[45:20] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and overlap; filler words present.
